analysis.one_liner: Replaces plant-by-plant power plant pollution limits with national cap-and-trade caps on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: after referral to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in March 2003, it never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clear Skies Act would have rewritten the Clean Air Act's power plant rules. It set national ceilings on sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from power plants and let companies trade emission allowances instead of meeting plant-by-plant limits. It also exempted plants covered by the trading program from the Clean Air Act's new-source review rules, which require older plants to install modern pollution controls when they upgrade, and it gave companies their allowances for free.
analysis.who_benefits: Downwind residents would gain from lower national pollution ceilings, especially for acid rain and fine particles. Coal- and oil-fired power plant operators would also gain: they would receive emission allowances free of charge, could buy extra allowances cheaply rather than install controls, and would escape new-source review requirements for covered units.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents and power plant operators

how_it_helps.text: Creates new national emission limits for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from power plants, extending the acid rain cap-and-trade model to more pollutants and sources.
Requires EPA to set performance standards for new boilers, gasification plants, and combustion turbines, and funds a research program on the health effects of fine particles and mercury.

Gives affected power plants a single predictable federal program instead of separate state and federal requirements, and lets units that opt in escape prevention-of-significant-deterioration and nonattainment review.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, power companies would have paid for allowances at auction or for emission controls, costs likely passed to electricity customers. People living near plants that buy allowances instead of installing controls could face locally concentrated pollution, a known risk when trading a pollutant like mercury that accumulates in fish near specific sources. The value of the free allowances would have gone to plant owners rather than the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Electricity customers and people near dirty plants

drawbacks.text: The bill excludes covered units from major-source prevention-of-significant-deterioration and nonattainment requirements, weakening the existing tool that forces old plants to modernize their controls when they rebuild or expand.
Allowances are allocated to owners without cost, so the right to pollute under the new caps is handed to power companies for free rather than auctioned for public revenue.

Turning mercury into a tradable allowance raises the risk that some communities near plants that buy allowances instead of controls would see little local reduction, because mercury settles near where it is emitted and accumulates in fish.
The national caps would not start binding until years after enactment, with the tightest limits deferred to 2018 and an EPA study deciding afterward whether they should be adjusted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered real reductions in three major pollutants, but on a slower timetable and with a weaker enforcement structure than the existing Clean Air Act rules it replaced: plant-specific new-source review would be traded away for free allowances and regional trading. Critics argued that, for plants that could buy cheap allowances instead of installing controls, the result could be more local pollution than current law allows; supporters argued a single national cap is more efficient and would still cut emissions substantially. Whether the trade favored the public depended heavily on where one lived relative to plants that chose to buy allowances rather than controls.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its energy subcommittee in March 2003, and nobody ever scheduled a hearing or vote, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Barton introduced the bill on February 27, 2003, for himself and Rep. Billy Tauzin, both 'by request,' the mechanism used when a bill is submitted at an outside requester's ask, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
On March 17, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and the action record shows no hearing, markup, or floor action afterward.
Only one member cosponsored the bill, a Republican, and the bill received no vote in either chamber before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Downwind residents and anyone protected by the existing new-source review rules are better off that the bill died, because the stricter plant-by-plant requirements stayed in force. Coal-fired power plant operators lost the chance at free allowances and an exemption from new-source review.

for.name: Bush administration
for.what_they_did: Proposed the Clear Skies plan as its preferred rewrite of the power plant rules; the bill was introduced 'by request,' consistent with an administration request.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Air Quality Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the March 2003 subcommittee referral; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired there.

against.name: Public health and environmental groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill, arguing it would replace enforceable plant-specific cleanup requirements with trading and exempt dirty plants from new-source review.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split was recorded; in the record the bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor and no Democratic support.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed national emission caps on power plants but given owners their allowances free of charge and exempted covered units from new-source review and nonattainment requirements, easing the existing pressure to retrofit old plants. Utilities could also buy extra allowances cheaply instead of installing controls.

The bill includes regulatory incentives for clean coal technology demonstration projects and sets up a trading system that keeps coal-fired generation operating under national caps rather than forcing plant retirements.

Trading lets some plants buy allowances instead of installing scrubbers and mercury controls, reducing the pool of mandated retrofits, though plants that cannot find cheap allowances would still need equipment. Performance standards for new units keep some demand in place.
